zone: Pasayten — Harts Pass, the upper Methow and the Craggies
_areas_note: THREE separate road systems feed this zone and they do not connect in the mountains. (1) The Harts Pass road out of Mazama (Lost River Road becoming Forest Road 5400) serves the Monument Creek trailhead at about mile 7, the Robinson Creek trailhead at about mile 9, and then climbs to Harts Pass and Slate Pass at nearly 7,000 ft — Robinson Mountain, Blackcap, Dot, Osceola, Ptarmigan, Monument Peak and Lake Mountain all hang off this road, either from the low valley trailheads or from the high start at Slate Pass. (2) The Pacific Crest Trail and the West Fork Pasayten River trail run north from Harts Pass itself and are the only legal United States approach to Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak, both of which sit within a few miles of the Canadian border 25 to 30 trail miles out. (3) Big Craggy and West Craggy are NOT on the Harts Pass road at all — they are reached from the Copper Glance trailhead on the Eightmile Creek road out of Winthrop by way of the Chewuch road, a completely different drainage and a different drive. They stay in this zone because the two Craggies share the eastern Pasayten trailhead cluster with the Billy Goat road, but a party cannot combine them with anything on the Harts Pass crest in one trip. NOTHING here duplicates the Cathedral and Amphitheater file, which covers the Andrews Creek and Iron Gate approaches on the far northeastern side of the wilderness — different road, different drainage, no shared camp. No peak was excluded; every one of the eleven has a defensible approach from a trailhead named above. Lake Mountain and Monument Peak were the closest call, since they are usually done from the Monument Creek trailhead low on the Harts Pass road rather than from the crest, and a party thinking of them as Harts Pass peaks will drive 13 miles too far.

sites.name: Harts Pass and Meadows campgrounds
sites.capacity: Two small Forest Service campgrounds a mile apart, five or six sites at the pass itself and roughly twice that at Meadows, first come first served with no reservations. They fill on summer weekends and in larch season, and there is no overflow up here.
sites.water: None. Neither campground has potable water and there is no piped supply anywhere on the pass, so haul everything up from the valley or plan on filtering from creeks well below. This is the single most common mistake parties make staging here.
sites.permit: Northwest Forest Pass or an Interagency pass to park at the trailheads; the campgrounds themselves are free but carry no services and no trash collection, so everything you bring comes back out. The free self-issue Pasayten wilderness permit is filled out at the trailhead kiosk before you walk in, not here. Campfires are legal in the existing rings when no burn ban is in effect, but the ground is thin alpine meadow and firewood is scarce, so most parties do without.
sites.notes: This is the staging ground for almost everything in the zone and the road to it is a substantial fact in its own right. Forest Road 5400 climbs roughly twenty miles of unpaved single lane from Mazama with pullouts rather than passing room, a rock wall on one side and an unguarded drop on the other, and grades approaching seventeen percent on the upper ramps. Trailers are prohibited outright and motorhomes and wide vehicles are strongly discouraged. The road opens with the snowmelt, typically early to mid July and occasionally not until later, and closes with the first serious autumn storms. Above the pass it continues to the gate below Slate Peak at about 7,440 feet, the highest driveable point in the state, which puts you at a trailhead where the walking starts near 7,000 feet instead of 2,500. Four trails leave from here — the Pacific Crest Trail, the West Fork Pasayten, the Middle Fork Pasayten and Buckskin Ridge — so this one pass is the door to Osceola, Blackcap, Dot, Ptarmigan, Castle and Blizzard. Nights are cold and wind at the pass is relentless; pitch behind timber rather than in the open meadow. Note that a large lightning fire that began in mid July 2026 closed the road above the Monument Creek trailhead along with much of the northern wilderness, so confirm the road is actually open before committing to a long drive.

sites.name: Windy Pass and the crest camps north of Harts Pass
sites.capacity: A string of small established sites in the meadows and basins along the crest, most taking one or two tents. The Pacific Crest Trail hiking season overlaps the climbing season, so expect company at the obvious ones and be ready to walk on to the next.
sites.water: Sparse and the defining planning problem of this stretch. There is nothing at the pass itself; the nearest campsites with water sit most of a mile further on and a couple of hundred feet higher. Carry enough for at least six miles at a time, and treat the basin between Foggy Pass and Windy Pass, the Shaw Creek crossing and the spring near Holman Peak as the fixed points to plan around rather than assuming you will find something in between.
sites.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Harts Pass, no quota and nothing to reserve. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Party size limits and any seasonal campfire ban are posted at the trailhead and change year to year, so read the board rather than assuming. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of any lake shoreline, and stock parties must carry certified weed-free feed and may not tie animals to trees overnight.
sites.notes: This is the first day of every trip toward Castle and Blizzard and the natural stop for anyone who wants a night high on the crest without a valley grind. The trail leaves Harts Pass at about 6,200 feet, tops out just under 7,000 a little over two miles north, and never drops below 5,000 the whole way to the border, so this is sustained high open country with long views and no shelter. Snow lingers on the north-facing traverses well into the summer and those crossings are the reason most parties wait until mid August in a heavy year. Wind is the standing complaint at Windy Pass and it earns the name; camping a little below the crest costs nothing and buys a great deal. There is no mobile service anywhere along here. As pure staging these camps do nothing for the Robinson Creek or Middle Fork peaks, which go the other direction from the pass.

sites.name: Hopkins Lake and Castle Pass
sites.capacity: Hopkins Lake holds several small established sites in the trees around the shore and is the most comfortable camp in the far north of the wilderness. Castle Pass itself has room for a couple of parties in the timber. Neither is large and both see through-hiker traffic.
sites.water: Hopkins Lake is the reliable one and is worth the descent for that reason alone — it is the best water for many miles in either direction. Castle Pass is drier and the sources near it are seasonal, so fill at the lake before continuing north.
sites.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Harts Pass. The international boundary matters here in a way it does not elsewhere in the zone: crossing north into Canada from the backcountry is not lawful and the long-standing arrangement that let northbound trail hikers walk out to the highway in British Columbia was ended in 2025, so there is no exit that way and no legal entry southbound either. Everything in this corner is now an out-and-back from Harts Pass. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline; pull back into the trees.
sites.notes: These are the camps that make Castle Peak and Blizzard Peak possible at all from the American side. Hopkins Lake sits about twenty-four trail miles north of Harts Pass, six hundred feet below the trail, and Castle Pass is roughly twenty-seven miles out at about 5,450 feet. Castle Peak rises directly north and east of the pass and is a scramble from a camp here; Blizzard Peak lies further east toward Frosty Pass and the Chuchuwanteen country and is more often reached by dropping down the West Fork Pasayten from Harts Pass instead, which is a different but comparably long line. Either way this is a three to five day trip for a fit party and there is no shortcut — the loss of the Canadian exit removed the only short approach that ever existed for these two summits. Plan food and water for the full round trip, expect snow on the north slopes into August, and understand that a weather change up here leaves you a very long way from the car.

sites.name: Robinson Creek valley campsites
sites.capacity: Nine established sites are spread along the trail at roughly one and a half, two and a half, four, six, six and a half, seven and a half and nine miles from the trailhead, so a party can pick its distance rather than racing to one spot. Most take one or two tents. Stock parties use this valley heavily.
sites.water: Good, and unusually so for this wilderness — the creek runs beside the trail for most of its length and most of the established sites hold water into the autumn. This is the one approach in the zone where water is not the limiting factor.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead kiosk, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Certified weed-free feed is required for stock and animals may not be tied directly to trees overnight or highlined within eight feet of them. Campfires are allowed in existing rings outside a burn ban, though the lower valley is dry and bans are common by late summer.
sites.notes: The trailhead sits at about 2,560 feet just off the Harts Pass road, which means this is the low road into country whose summits stand near 8,500 — the elevation gain is the whole story. Robinson Mountain is climbed from here by walking a little over two miles to the Beauty Creek bridge and picking up an unmaintained path just beyond it, then leaving that for open slopes above; it is fourteen miles round trip with over six thousand feet of gain and only very fit parties do it in a day, so a first night at one of the lower established sites is the sensible plan. Carrying on up the valley reaches Robinson Pass at 6,220 feet in about nine and a half miles and drops into the Middle Fork Pasayten, which is the back door to Blackcap and Osceola for anyone who would rather not start from Slate Pass. The lower valley burns and reburns, so expect open hot walking, standing dead timber and variable blowdown, and note that this drainage was inside the 2026 fire closure. Ask the district about trail conditions before building a schedule around it.

sites.name: Doris Lake and Freds Lake basins
sites.capacity: Informal sites on benches and ridge shoulders back from the water, room for two or three small parties without crowding. Nothing developed, no tables, no toilets.
sites.water: Both lakes hold through the season and are the dependable supply for this whole group of peaks. Between them and the Middle Fork river flats a party can plan a multi-day traverse without rationing, which is not true of most of this wilderness.
sites.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Harts Pass, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camp at least a hundred feet back from either shoreline — the ground close to the water is thin and already worn. Weed-free feed for stock, and no tying animals to trees overnight.
sites.notes: This is the working climbers' camp for Osceola Peak and Blackcap Mountain and the first night of the long traverse that links them with Carru and Lago. The line in starts high, which is the point: from Slate Pass at about 6,900 feet a short connector drops to the Middle Fork Pasayten trail, five miles of valley walking leads to the Ferguson Lake spur, and three more miles of climbing reaches Doris Lake at just under 7,000 feet. Osceola is then a short cross-country scramble northeast through open forest from camp, which is as close as anything in the Pasayten comes to convenient. Blackcap is further along the ridge system and is usually taken on the second or third day. Freds Lake sits on the parallel line toward Rolo Pass and serves the same purpose for parties heading for Shellrock. Reckon on three to four days for anything based here and remember that the return from a high camp means regaining Slate Pass at the end. Larches turn in the last week of September and the first of October, which is also when the nights get genuinely cold at this elevation.

sites.name: Shellrock Pass, Shellrock Basin and the Eureka Creek meadows
sites.capacity: Dispersed rather than designated. There is a forested site by the creek at about 5,800 feet where the old Eureka Creek trail joins, a broad spread of good ground in the Eureka Creek meadows near 6,300 feet, and open camping around the pond in Shellrock Basin. Several parties can spread out through this country without seeing each other.
sites.water: Reliable at the creek camp and in the Eureka meadows, and the pond in Shellrock Basin usually holds. The passes themselves are dry, so fill in the basin or the meadows before going up rather than expecting to find snowmelt on the crest late in the season.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek. Stock use is significant through here — weed-free feed is required and animals may not be tied to trees overnight. Fires are legal outside a ban but the meadows are fragile and most parties cook on a stove and leave it at that.
sites.notes: Shellrock is the camp for Ptarmigan Peak and Dot Mountain, both of which are otherwise out of reach. The standard line leaves Slate Pass, follows the Middle Fork Pasayten to Berk Creek, climbs to Freds Pass and crosses the head of Eureka Creek to Shellrock Pass, which puts a party in position to scramble Ptarmigan the following day; Dot is taken from the same country on the way through, usually in combination with the Lago and Carru group. This is genuinely remote — thirty-five miles and thirteen thousand feet of gain over four days is a fair description of a trip that collects three or four summits here — and there is no short version. The meadow ground is soft and holds a footprint for years, so pitch on the timber edge or on gravel rather than in the open grass. Snow lingers on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the single biggest constraint on when this is worth attempting.

sites.name: Lake of the Woods and the Eureka Falls camp
sites.capacity: Lake of the Woods is a small alpine basin with room for a couple of tents on the benches below Lake Mountain. The Eureka Falls site down in the valley near the confluence of the Lost River and Eureka Creek is a forested camp taking a party or two. Neither is developed.
sites.water: The lake is dependable and so is Eureka Creek down in the valley. Between them, though, is the crux: the creek crossing about four miles in is the last certain water before an eight-mile climb gaining five thousand feet to the pass, and in a hot late-summer spell that carry is what makes or breaks the day. Fill completely at the creek.
sites.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit at the Monument Creek trailhead kiosk, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. Camping is prohibited within a hundred feet of the lake shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, and the usual prohibition on tying animals to trees overnight.
sites.notes: This is the camp for Monument Peak and Lake Mountain and it is worth being clear that they are approached from a completely different point on the Harts Pass road than the crest peaks — the Monument Creek trailhead at about 2,400 feet, roughly seven miles up from Mazama, thirteen miles short of the pass. The route runs up the Lost River valley, crosses Eureka Creek where the bridge has been out in the past, then climbs the abandoned Pistol Ridge trail to Pistol Pass at 7,100 feet before dropping to the lake. Expect around thirty miles and thirteen thousand feet over three to four days for both summits — Monument at 8,592 feet by its south ridge, Lake Mountain at 8,371 by its east ridge, each a short steep scramble from the basin. The Pistol Ridge trail is unmaintained and route-finding through it is part of the work. An alternative for parties coming from the north is to drop off Lake Mountain into Eureka Creek and camp near the south fork, which shortens things considerably if the traverse is already underway. Late September brings the larches and cold clear nights; earlier in the summer the long dry climb to the pass is punishing.

sites.name: Copper Glance Lake
sites.capacity: One good area at the lake taking three or four tents. That is the whole of it, so a busy autumn weekend can fill it and there is no obvious second choice nearby.
sites.water: The lake, and it is reliable. This is the only certain water high on the approach, since the trail above the old mine works is dry through the meadows.
sites.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit at the trailhead, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at the Copper Glance trailhead. Camp back from the shoreline rather than on it. The lower trail passes old mine workings on patented ground — leave the structures and hardware alone.
sites.notes: This is the only camp that serves Big Craggy and West Craggy, and it belongs to a different drive from everything else in this zone: north from Winthrop on the West Chewuch road, then left onto the Eightmile Creek road and about twelve to thirteen miles to the trailhead at 3,800 feet. Nothing here connects to Harts Pass on foot. The trail climbs steeply for roughly two and a half miles on an old gated mining road past a washed-out bridge and the mine, then becomes a real trail through meadows on the shoulder of Big Craggy to the lake at 6,100 feet. A strong party can car-camp low on the Eightmile Creek road at one of the small Forest Service campgrounds along the creek and take both summits in one long day of about twelve miles and five thousand eight hundred feet, leaving the trail near 5,900 feet for Big Craggy's southeast ridge, then descending to the 7,600 foot saddle and picking a gully onto West Craggy's east ridge. Camping at the lake instead breaks that into something far more pleasant. The upper scree is loose and tiring on the ascent. This is an east-side approach and melts out earlier than the crest, but snow still holds above 5,500 feet well into the early summer, and the Eightmile Creek country has burned repeatedly in recent years so shade and blowdown are both unpredictable.
